policy: Even multiple Fathers at one Scripture location do not necessarily address one identical question. Keep each answer as a verbatim pointer into its own Catena source and distinguish allegory, reported opponent, doctrinal condition and alternative readings.

groups.modernReaderQuestion: How can Christ's yoke be easy if following Him demands sacrifice?
groups.analyticalComparison: Gregory refers to relief from disordered desire; Rabanus to love's developing sweetness; Jerome contrasts Gospel and Law.
groups.sourceDifferenceOrRisk: Do not suggest the texts all address exactly the same sense of 'easy'; Jerome's law-and-grace wording needs contextual theological scrutiny.

groups.modernReaderQuestion: What should Christians learn from the wheat and tares about separating evil from good?
groups.analyticalComparison: Jerome addresses rash expulsion and apparent ambiguity; Chrysostom comments on order of final gathering; Augustine offers and then qualifies a heresy-bundle interpretation.
groups.sourceDifferenceOrRisk: Preserve Augustine's retraction/qualification. Avoid treating church discipline and final divine judgment as interchangeable.

groups.modernReaderQuestion: Why did Peter sink, and what does Christ's rescue teach?
groups.analyticalComparison: Augustine emphasizes Peter's prayer and an allegory of the Church; Chrysostom contrasts the physical wind with weakness of faith.
groups.sourceDifferenceOrRisk: The Church-as-Peter interpretation must remain marked as Augustine's allegory, not an additional literal Gospel event.

groups.modernReaderQuestion: Why does Christ oppose some traditions of the elders?
groups.analyticalComparison: Chrysostom distinguishes accusation based on human tradition rather than Mosaic law; Jerome stresses material support owed to parents.
groups.sourceDifferenceOrRisk: The Pharisees' historical question belongs to the Gospel speakers, not to Chrysostom or Jerome.

groups.modernReaderQuestion: What does Christ mean by the plant not planted by the Father?
groups.analyticalComparison: Chrysostom rejects identifying the uprooted plant with the Mosaic Law; Jerome develops an account of God's planting and the will's possible deviation.
groups.sourceDifferenceOrRisk: Do not equate Chrysostom's refutation of Manichaeans with Jerome's account of free will as if they were a single argument.

groups.modernReaderQuestion: Why does Christ use bread and leaven to teach the disciples?
groups.analyticalComparison: Chrysostom offers reasons for the figurative rebuke and its timing; Jerome explains lack of bread and distinguishes corrupt teaching from wholesome doctrine.
groups.sourceDifferenceOrRisk: A topic group may contain several questions, so use subquestions or separate bubbles with distinct original answer anchors.

groups.modernReaderQuestion: Why does Christ ask who people say the Son of Man is?
groups.analyticalComparison: Jerome discusses the wording and humility of the question; Chrysostom distinguishes popular opinion from hostile opponents; Hilary insists on Christ's humanity and divinity.
groups.sourceDifferenceOrRisk: The literal question was asked by Christ and must not be re-presented as though Jerome, Hilary or Chrysostom originally asked it.
